title: Every Diamond Shines: Oracy, Culture, and the Classroom Orchestra
author: Anisa Khan
source: adamkohlbeck.substack.com (Teaching on Purpose, guest post), October 30, 2026
summary: In a guest post for Adam Kohlbeck's Teaching on Purpose, sociology teacher Anisa Khan describes how routines, high expectations and oracy build a classroom culture in which every student is seen and heard. She compares the classroom to an orchestra and argues that student voice is a right under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, not an add-on. Consistent routines such as greeting students, pronouncing every name correctly and 'signal, pause, insist' make her a safe, reliable adult, and her 'diamond mantra' links high standards with real relationships. She says purposeful routines let talk flourish rather than derail lessons, and lists tools including choral response, cold and warm calling, and ABC questioning (Agree, Build, Challenge), with worked examples from sociology and health and social care using relatable cues like reality TV. She also describes founding a school debate society and argues that high standards and inclusion are two sides of the same coin. The post is personal and practice-focused, so it sits in Practice and Culture.
points: Routines, consistency and meaning what you say make a teacher a 'safe person', which is the foundation for psychological safety and risk-taking.
Structured routines are what let classroom talk flourish; ABC questioning (Agree, Build, Challenge) gives every student a way into the conversation.
Viable cues drawn from pop culture, such as the Kardashians as a longitudinal study, work only if the teacher first supplies the context so no student is excluded.
A single question can be laddered up Bloom's taxonomy from recall to create, as in the middle adulthood life stages example.
A school debate society extends oracy beyond lessons, and Khan frames high standards and inclusion as inseparable.
quotes: In many ways, a classroom is like an orchestra: every voice matters, and the real magic happens when harmony, uniqueness, and purpose blend.
Oracy is not an “add-on”—it is the thread that weaves belonging, behaviour, and relationships into the fabric of every school day.

Consistency is not about perfection, but about reliability. Over time, students learn that expectations are transparent and fair—because they see it in action every day, from a teacher who walks the talk.

Some colleagues may worry that too much discussion can derail progress; in my experience, it is purposeful routines—signals, transitions, and boundaries—that actually enable talk to flourish, making questioning and dialogue both intuitive and inclusive.

These strategies, drawn from debate protocols and dialogic teaching, ensure that all students have structured ways to enter the conversation, think out loud, develop their reasoning, and learn from one another—with the teacher at the heart of it all, navigating the flow and supporting every voice.
One important reflection from my early training is not to assume all students will know a pop culture reference, however well-intentioned.

Oracy and culture are mutually reinforcing: cultures of trust and belonging create the space for student voice and questioning to thrive, and what we communicate—verbally, non-verbally, through our instruction, planning, and feedback—shapes the classroom ecosystem in profound ways.

Hope is not naïve; it is the everyday, deliberate act of believing in the possibility of belonging, voice, and aspiration for every student—even when that hope is tested by the contextual realities, pressures, and barriers we face as educators.
